title: The Two Bags
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: Every man carries Two Bags about with him, one in front and one behind, and both are packed full of faults. The Bag in front contains his neighbours' faults, the one behind his own. Hence it is that men do not see their own faults, but never fail to see those of others.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how many bags does every man carry?
According to the passage, where is one of the bags positioned?
According to the passage, what do both bags contain?
According to the passage, whose faults are in the bag in front?
According to the passage, whose faults are in the bag behind?
According to the passage, what do men fail to see about themselves?
Based on the passage, why can't a man easily see the bag behind him?
options: It is much smaller than the bag in front
It is locked shut so no one can see inside
It is only visible to other people, not the man himself
It is positioned out of his own line of sight, unlike the one he can see in front

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the placement of the two bags explain about human behavior?
options: Why people always carry more belongings than they need
Why people notice others' flaws so easily while overlooking their own
Why people prefer walking in pairs rather than alone
Why people trust strangers more than their neighbors

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "faults" mean in "both are packed full of faults"?
Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: People are quick to notice others' flaws while remaining blind to their own
Everyone should examine their neighbours' faults before judging their own
Carrying too many belongings makes people forgetful
Faults are equally visible to everyone who has them

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who is said to carry these two bags?
According to the passage, what word describes how full the bags are?
According to the passage, what do men "never fail" to do?
Based on the passage, what would likely happen if the two bags were swapped in position?
options: A man might become more aware of his own faults and less focused on others'
Nothing would change, since the bags contain the same things regardless
The bags would become impossible to carry at all
Neighbours would no longer have any faults to notice

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the image of carrying bags suggest about how faults are treated?
options: Faults are rare and only a few people actually have them
Faults can be permanently discarded once noticed
Faults only exist in the imagination of others
Faults are something everyone carries as a natural, unavoidable part of life

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "Hence" mean in "Hence it is that men do not see their own faults"?
Which of these best summarizes what the passage describes?
options: A story about a man who loses one of his two bags
A warning against carrying too many belongings while travelling
An image of two bags explaining why people notice others' faults but not their own
An argument that faults should never be discussed openly
